revisions.title: Nature, convention, and the price of instruction
revisions.body: At the opening of the inquiry, two accounts of naming are placed in view: names are correct by nature, or they are correct by convention. The passage also contrasts a one-drachma lesson with Prodicus’ fifty-drachma course.

The fee contrast gives the discussion a practical scale: ordinary instruction is set against Prodicus’ fifty-drachma course. It highlights the differing prices attached to instruction without deciding the naming question itself.
Stay with the assent chain itself: each concession narrows what can be claimed, so the force of the analysis lies in the sequence of granted steps rather than in an added illustrative case.
Keep the conclusion at the scale of this refutation: the argument points toward the importance of stable being for assessing names, but it does not by itself ground the whole inquiry into names.

revisions.title: The carpenter’s shuttle
revisions.body: Socrates’s craft analogy uses a carpenter as the maker of the shuttle. Keeping that trade accurate matters: the comparison concerns how a tool is made for its function, not a smith’s work.

The etymological proposal is best treated as a hypothesis, not a verdict: a derivation may make a name intelligible without yet showing that the name fits the thing. It advances the inquiry while leaving its conclusion open.
The examples remain qualified: names are often inherited from ancestors, while many are chosen in accordance with parental wishes; neither practice is presented as universal.
Socrates declines to pursue divine naming here and limits the inquiry to what human beings say about names. This move does not yield divine etymologies.

revisions.title: The Motion-Based Etymologies
revisions.body: The motion-based etymologies form a coherent cluster: they repeatedly connect the names with movement and change. That pattern is the point to retain; it does not by itself warrant a historical attribution to the name-givers.

revisions.title: Representation Is Not Duplication
revisions.body: The painting comparison has a narrower use than a general account of name quality: it tests whether representing a thing requires reproducing it in every respect. The analogy thus separates depiction from identity, leaving the representation answerable to its subject without making the two indistinguishable.
The dialogue ends with Socrates’ commitment to the Heraclitean view that all things are in motion.
